articles.title: Eurovision took its song contest to Asia – bringing its political drama and cultural tropes along for the ride
articles.author: Paul David Flood, Assistant Professor of Musicology, University of Tennessee
paras: ABBA and Céline Dion came to the world’s attention thanks to the Eurovision Song Contest, an annual showcase of pop music, camp and spectacle.

Filipino singer Carmelle is hoping that the Eurovision Song Contest Asia will serve as a similar springboard to international fame. On Nov. 14, 2026, Carmelle bested entries from 11 Asian countries to be crowned the Asian edition’s first-ever winner. The competition marked Eurovision’s boldest expansion of its format in its 70-year history.

As a scholar of contemporary European popular music and politics, I study the ways in which Eurovision shapes notions of what it looks like and sounds like to be European. Knowing that the Asian edition would be organized by European broadcasting executives, I wanted to see how closely Eurovision Asia would resemble the flagship Eurovision, or whether it would carve out an identity of its own.

Eurovision’s proposed expansion into Asia dates back to 2008, when the European Broadcasting Union – the transnational coalition of public service media organizations that has organized the Eurovision Song Contest since 1956 – announced plans for “Our Sound – The Asia-Pacific Song Contest.” Originally slated to debut in 2010, the project never materialized.

On March 31, 2026, however, Voxovation, a European-led production company that oversees the development of Eurovision’s spinoffs, announced that Bangkok would host the inaugural Asian competition in partnership with Thailand’s Channel 3 and S2O Productions.
Eurovision Asia is now the second European Broadcasting Union-licensed global spinoff to make the airwaves.
In 2022, Voxovation organized the American Song Contest, which included original songs by artists from all 50 U.S. states, five territories and Washington.

Despite being promoted to the American public in a Super Bowl commercial featuring hosts Kelly Clarkson and Snoop Dogg, the competition failed to attract a large viewership and the spinoff wasn’t renewed.

Given two decades of uncertainty, as well as the failure of Voxovation’s U.S. spinoff, some critics doubted whether the Asian version would succeed. And for a moment, it looked like everything might fall apart: In late October 2026, the Swedish newspaper Aftonbladet reported that Eurovision Asia’s original budget of approximately US$4.5 million had been reduced by US$1 million.

The European Broadcasting Union, however, confirmed that the show would go on as planned, and at 8:30 p.m. Bangkok time on Nov. 14, the show’s two hosts, Thai media personalities Woody Milintachinda and Cindy Bishop, welcomed viewers from around the world tuning in via television broadcast and the YouTube livestream.
“Maybe you’ve never heard of Eurovision before, or maybe you’re one of the hardcore Eurofans,” said Bishop. “It doesn’t matter, because you will be blown away by the talent here tonight!”
For the next two-and-a-half hours, each country’s representative performed an original song, with Vietnam’s Tóc Tiên opening the show with her song “Em Tiên” (“Fairy Maiden”).

Vietnam’s entry had many of the spectacular ingredients of an ideal Eurovision entry: bilingual lyrics, large props, flashy outfits and a dance break. The song’s instrumentation included a flute accompanying Tiên’s melody and a bamboo xylophone. It concluded with a second, high-energy dance break reminiscent of electronic dance music genres.

The song’s use of traditional Asian musical signifiers followed the approach of the European entrants that have incorporated folk traditions to promote their national cultures to an international audience.

For example, Ukraine’s 2004 winning entry, Ruslana’s “Wild Dances,” opened with the trembita, a long alpine horn associated with the Hutsul people of the Carpathian Mountains. Armenia’s 2008 entry, Sirusho’s “Qele, Qele,” similarly combined a traditional Armenian duduk flute, zurna trumpet and dhol drums with an upbeat dance track and contemporary pop vocals. While some scholars claim that these musical gestures strategically romanticize and exoticize regional cultures, it’s a way to fuse national identity with modern music.

Other Eurovision Asia entrants also pulled from this playbook. Mongolia’s singer, Beck, wore a deel, the country’s traditional robe, while performing. He also incorporated a traditional Mongolian string instrument into his performance.

Voting, which was open to the general public via an online form, began just before the first performance. Viewers were allotted eight free votes, on the condition that they had to vote for at least three different countries. They could purchase 10 additional votes. The public accounted for half the votes, while a jury made up of representatives from each nation accounted for the other half.

Carmelle’s winning song – a Filipina women’s empowerment anthem titled “Sobra-Sobra” (“Too Much”) – featured a repeated musical line played by a kulintang, a Filipino percussion instrument, and a frenetic dance break. The song’s bridge was rapped in Tagalog, the country’s national language.
As part of her reward, Carmelle will perform “Sobra-Sobra” at the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest in Burgas, Bulgaria.
No Eurovision competition would be complete without a measure of political controversy.

From broadcaster boycotts over Israel’s participation amid the war in Gaza to suspicions that Franco’s Spain rigged the 1968 Eurovision vote in its favor, political disputes have long been part of the competition.

Normally, political statements are not permitted in Eurovision, though exceptions have been made for humanitarian causes. Ukraine’s victory in Eurovision 2022 took place just a few months after Russia’s full-scale invasion of the former Soviet republic. Oleh Psiuk, the frontman of Ukraine’s entrant, Kalush Orchestra, pleaded for support for Ukraine at the end of the performance, which the European Broadcasting Union ended up allowing.
During Eurovision Song Contest Asia, Malaysia found itself at the center of controversy.

Malaysian entrant Aina Abdul, who wears a hijab in her public appearances, performed her song “Bluest Sky.” While Abdul was seen as a possible favorite, Malaysian audiences claimed that she ultimately did not score enough points due to Islamophobia.

Another controversy arose due to the Malaysian broadcaster TV3’s coverage of the show. During the results segment at the end of the show, the camera feed of the Filipino spokesperson, the drag queen Vice Ganda, was cut from the Malaysian broadcast. Malaysian broadcasting laws restrict the airing of drag and LGBTQ+ content on television, radio and digital platforms.
In a comment to The Guardian, Eurovision Director Martin Green said, “We are surprised and disappointed to learn that the broadcast of Eurovision Song Contest Asia was altered in Malaysia.”
“We take this matter seriously and will be writing to Voxovation,” Green added.
TV3 has yet to comment on the incident.

Here, there are also echoes of the European competition: Eurovision has embraced multicultural and pro-LGBTQ+ values to such an extent that countries like Hungary and Turkey have withdrawn due to their governments’ incompatible sociopolitical values.
Eurovision Asia’s controversies prove that the European Broadcasting Union has a new – perhaps unexpected – set of geopolitical and sociopolitical values to navigate.

Television viewership for Eurovision Asia varied by market. In Vietnam, the show reached over 5 million viewers. The host country’s broadcast, however, only reached an average of 385,000 Thai viewers. These numbers pale in comparison to Eurovision 2026’s viewership of 131 million viewers across the 35 competing nations.

Nonetheless, hype is already building for the 2027 edition of Eurovision Asia. During a news conference in Bangkok, Voxovation executive Christer Björkman confirmed that multiple cities have expressed interest in hosting, with China, Japan and Taiwan indicating that they’re open to participating in the future.

If more Asian broadcasters buy in, Eurovision will attract an even larger international audience, bringing Voxovation one step closer to turning the contest from a European tradition into a global phenomenon.
But time will tell whether Eurovision Asia can become something more than a European competition staged elsewhere.

articles.title: Oscar Wilde had a surprising rapport with Colorado miners – why it is hard to imagine that happening today
articles.author: Joshua Fagan, PhD Candidate in 19th Century British Literature, University of Washington
paras: Oscar Wilde, the Victorian writer of “The Picture of Dorian Gray” and “The Importance of Being Earnest,” was a fashionable icon known as much for his refined manner and conversation as for his writings.
So the image of Wilde exploring Colorado’s frontier towns and rugged mines sounds like a scene from a dream. But that is exactly what happened during his extensive tour of the U.S. in 1882.
Wilde arrived in the U.S. from Europe with much aplomb. The impresario Richard D’Oyly Carte, the promoter of the acclaimed operetta duo W.S. Gilbert and Arthur Sullivan, bankrolled Wilde’s tour.

Gilbert and Sullivan had recently written a new comic opera, “Patience,” which mocked the aesthetic movement, of which Wilde was an icon. Championing artifice and refinement in all aspects of life, aesthetes dressed in ornate, unusual ways, such as Wilde’s habit of wearing an unnatural green carnation on his lapel. The often-mocked figure of the dandy, a wealthy man who dressed in the most bizarre and fanciful fashions of day, was an inspiration for aesthetes.

I study 19th-century literature in the English-speaking world, and I see Wilde’s western journey to my home state of Colorado as an example of how intellectual writers in the Victorian era were interested in the working class and how that curiosity was, perhaps surprisingly, mutual.
Wilde’s journey to the ‘Wild West’

Carte brought Wilde to America around the time of the U.S. premiere of “Patience” to help popularize the idea of the aesthete. While on tour, Wilde visited major cities, such as New York and Philadelphia, giving almost 100 interviews. But he also was interested in the “Wild West.” His curiosity may seem paradoxical: Tawdry saloons and dusty main streets were a stark contrast to the atmosphere of luxurious refinement he cultivated.

Yet, above all, Wilde craved the novel and unexpected. He sought experiences and people who were the opposite of the conventionality he saw as chaining Victorian society. The slightly anarchic roughness of the West appealed to him. He called it “the most beautiful part” of the country.

Wilde arrived in Colorado Springs in April 1882. Railroad baron William Jackson Palmer had founded this booming resort town in 1871. The town, a short railway journey from Denver, served as a health retreat for those suffering from tuberculosis – one of the deadliest diseases in the nation at the time.

Befitting its growing popularity, Colorado Springs had a thriving arts scene. According to the Colorado Springs Pioneers Museum, “interest in the arts began almost immediately” and was distinguished by the opening of an opera house in 1881. Crafting it in red brick and sandstone, the architects took inspiration from Madison Square Theater in New York. It became one of the most impressive buildings in the state.

Wilde gave his lecture on “The Decorative Arts” at this opera house. He did not condescend to his Colorado audience, nor did he suggest that the highest quality art could only exist in the refined settings of Europe. Instead, he insisted that art should be a part of ordinary existence.

“Art,” he declared, “is not something which you can take or leave” but rather “a necessity of human life.” For Wilde, art meant “value to the workman” and “the pleasure which he must necessarily take in making a beautiful thing.” The quality of art for Wilde was not about luxury and extravagance but about creativity and honesty in creation.

The local paper, The Daily Gazette – now The Gazette – reviewed his talk positively in a column from April 15, 1882. The column praises Wilde for how “the entire evening he commanded the closest attention of his audience.” Reportedly, when he “would give expression to a brilliant thought or idea a murmur of applause would pass through the audience.” The article finishes by exclaiming that the lecture “was instructive and interesting and appreciated by all who were present.”
Wilde’s popularity in the West reveals the oversimplistic nature of the divide between the “highbrow” culture of the literati and the culture of “common” society.

His visit to the isolated, high-elevation mountain town of Leadville makes this blending of “high” and “low” culture even more vital. In this hardscrabble town, which owed its existence to the hard labor of miners, workers came to the Tabor Opera House to hear the lavish aesthete. Similar to his speech in Colorado Springs, he discussed how “beautiful and rational designs are necessary in all work.”
For Wilde, the roughness of his surroundings were closer to his ideal than the conventionality of Eastern U.S. cities, with their “bad wall-papers horribly designed.”
The relationship between Wilde and his Leadville audience was symbiotic. The artist found what he desired in the hard-edged mountain town, far from the pomp and conventions of Europe.
“The revolver was their book of etiquette,” Wilde wrote of the town, not altogether disapprovingly.
He drank with miners, some of whom lowered him into the depths of the Matchless Mine, a riotous atmosphere he found rather exciting.
The miners, he wrote in his “Impressions of America,” were “very charming and not at all rough.” According to Wilde, these miners likewise found value in his discussions about art.
Beyond the ‘highbrow-lowbrow’ divide

Newspaper articles about Wilde’s lectures in Colorado do not emphasize the cultural gap between him and his audiences. That dynamic may not have seemed odd – other than the novelty of a foreign celebrity visiting towns in the interior of the country.

In addition, 19th-century literary culture may not have conceived of the rigid divide between highbrow literati interests and those of the working class that exists today. The historian Lawrence Levine, in his influential 1990 book “Highbrow/Lowbrow,” asserts that supposedly elite pursuits actually had wide appeal in 19th-century American culture.

For instance, opera was not associated primarily with multimillionaires in fancy tuxedos and evening gowns, but was also a popular pastime for all ages and social classes. That opera houses even existed in the frontier towns of Colorado demonstrates Levine’s point.
Working-class residents of Leadville appreciated the chance to hear Wilde lecture about art as much as he relished the chance to travel to a real mining town and talk with its residents.

In my view, economic and cultural divides of today can be bridged so everyone can engage intellectual insights and reflections. Witty, sophisticated authors like Wilde do not simply belong to exclusive elite circles.

articles.title: Elizabeth Holmes went from a startup darling to powerful seductress – these gendered portrayals profited investors
articles.author: Kate Kenny, Professor of Organization Studies, University of Galway
paras: Despite the countless books, podcasts, TV miniseries and documentaries, people continue to be fascinated by the fall of Elizabeth Holmes and her health-tech startup Theranos. We are now being offered a new insight into the founder through the much-hyped documentary, You Can See Everything.

The initial drama of the documentary takes places 34 days before Holmes started her 11-year prison sentence for investor fraud in 2023. In our research, we examined how Holmes was presented across promotional materials, tweets, talks and interviews over the ten year period from her initial appearance on the public stage in 2013 to the same period in which the documentary begins.

Valued at around US$9 billion (£7 billion) at its peak in 2014, Theranos claimed to have built a device that could run hundreds of lab tests from just a few drops of blood. Holmes and co-founder Sunny Balwani hid that the device could not in fact do what they said, leading to its 2018 shutdown and their convictions for investor fraud (and, in Balwani’s case, defrauding patients as well).

For many, the fascination in Holmes’s story lies in the hubris and deception of this young woman who set out to upend the multi-billion dollar diagnostic industry. But popular perspectives on Holmes obscure something important about how we view entrepreneurs, who we celebrate (or vilify) and whose interests this serves. This is something our research explores.
A highly sellable female entrepreneur
In our analysis, we found that gendered stereotypes helped create an attractive female narrative around Theranos and Holmes between 2013 and 2015 that served (predominantly male) investor interests.

Holmes was introduced as a very specific kind of woman entrepreneur – confident, ambitious, authoritative. The prominent venture capitalist Tim Draper, who made his name backing companies like Tesla and was an early investor in Theranos, praised what he saw as Holmes’s entrepreneurial instincts in 2014. He said she was the first entrepreneur he know who kept quiet about her business “so that the competition wouldn’t get a chance to start … She had a winner and knew it”.
In 2015, Theranos board member and longtime Holmes supporter former US secretary of state Henry Kissinger talked about her as combining “fierce and single-minded dedication with great charm”.
Much was also made of her looks, with the media often noting she was a “young, blond, and blue-eyed” woman. She was a refreshing change from the usual men the industry pinned all its hopes on.

Holmes did present a highly sellable vision of a new Silicon Valley that welcomed and celebrated female entrepreneurs. In her 2019 book The Code: Silicon Valley and the Remaking of America, tech historian Margaret O’Mara noted that Holmes’s rise coincided with growing public scrutiny of Silicon Valley’s lack of diversity, and the “tech-bro” homogeneity of the early-to-mid 2010s. At the time, the Valley was also beset by high profile gender discrimination cases.
For investors, Holmes was an attractive answer to a media problem the tech industry had and the media coverage of her rise certainly helped counter some of critics of the Valley’s “brotopia”.

But Holmes’s brand of female founder was not totally new and this also served investors. In many articles she was portrayed as the female reincarnation of the stereotypical “tech bro” – a Mark Zuckerberg with a heart or a Steve Jobs with a social consciousness.

Then there was her intentional self styling, which the media played up as symbols central to her status as a female tech-visionary. Holmes’s signature black turtle necks seemed to be a homage to the uniform of Jobs, who regularly wore an Issey Miyake black turtleneck. She was asked about it again and again, admitting in an interview with Glamour that she owned 150 of them.

Holmes’s founder uniform combined with the fact that she had dropped out of university to pursue her vision, like Jobs, Zuckerberg and Bill Gates, gave her many of the recognisable characteristics of a successful tech founder. She was like all these visionaries but with the added bonus of being a woman. This portrayal fed straight into investor interests by making Holmes at once both familiar and novel, helping her company Theranos’s value to climb to unprecedented heights.

However, when things started to turn sour, our research found that much less flattering gendered stereotypes were quickly deployed. These narratives framed Holmes’ downfall as female weakness in order to protect powerful men.
Holmes was vilified, not only as a failed entrepreneur, but also as a seductress who had used specifically female charms to lead competent men astray.

According to Rolling Stone, she “lured” male investors into her fraudulent schemes. Meanwhile, the Evening Standard reported her as having “wooed” the men on her board to do her bidding. Financial journalists described how Holmes “dazzled” normally sober leaders at supermarket chains Walgreens and Safeway who then invested in her scheme.

Holmes’s board of directors – once portrayed as the “most illustrious board in US corporate history” – along with the other powerful men she was seen as having duped could now be presented as innocent victims of malicious female magic.

For investors, this villification of Holmes could help them spin their own narratives in order to preserve public trust in their abilities. They could argue that her monstrous supernatural abilities to bamboozle and manipulate were too strong for them to overcome. In this media framing, the fact that investors appeared not to have conducted basic due diligence before investing hundreds of millions of dollars was neither their fault nor a reflection of their real talent for investment. They were simply good men who wanted to help people but had been fooled by a woman playing on an emotional blind spot. They were credulous rather than gullible.

To be clear, we don’t excuse Holmes or seek to diminish the seriousness of what she did. But her story tells us something interesting about the wider system surrounding tech entrepreneurs, and how we can remain blind to the ways capital interests can fuel – and exploit – popular and idolised archetypes.

You Can See Everything provides a new intimate portrait of Holmes, which will add, change or warp ideas we already have about her. But we also need to turn the focus back onto ourselves and think about the ways in which we idolise or judge people in her position – and the gendered stereotypes we would rather not admit to holding.

articles.title: The philosophical reason AI Christmas ads leave audiences feeling cold
articles.author: Alex Fisher, Postdoctoral Fellow, University of Leeds
paras: It’s that time of year when Christmas adverts start appearing, and brands offer up a slice of consumerist comfort as you curl up in front of a screen.

Yet companies are increasingly using artificial intelligence (AI) to produce their ads. Last year proved how quickly that strategy can backfire. In the Netherlands, McDonald’s pulled an AI-generated Christmas ad depicting chaotic holiday mishaps after just three days following fierce backlash over the undisclosed usage.

This kind of omission is now restricted under new EU transparency rules that govern how AI-generated content is labelled. Coca-Cola’s 2025 festive campaign drew similar criticism. The advert featured AI-generated scenery and animals that many viewers found uncanny.

Undeterred, this year brands including Very and Plusnet have pressed ahead with AI productions. Because UK law does not require on-screen disclosure, their use of the technology is often tucked away in separate press releases and trade announcements rather than flagged to viewers. Even so, the UK Advertising Standards Authority prohibits misleading omissions if an advert falsely implies human creation to deceive consumers.

Other brands are more subtle with their AI use. While Royal Mail’s 2025 Christmas ad relied on traditional live-action footage, it recently emerged that the campaign used an AI voiceover to narrate the spot.

Replacing human performers – even behind the microphone – has fuelled growing anxiety among both industry insiders and the general public, echoing the fears that sparked the 2023 Hollywood writers’ and actors’ strikes.
Losing trust in animated ads

This growing scepticism means even traditional animation is no longer safe from scrutiny. Dior’s Christmas short film, for example, has generated suspicions among some viewers. Described as hand-drawn and directed by French animator Sylvain Chomet, with an all-star cast featuring Rihanna and Robert Pattinson, it centres on the fashion designer Christian Dior’s friendship with film star Marlene Dietrich.

Commenters praised its authentic visual appearance, while a behind the scenes page was published on Dior’s website highlighting the actors and design sketches, warding off accusations of AI-generation.

Despite this, some viewers believed that Dior’s advert showed several hallmarks of AI. A telltale sign of AI-generated content is garbled hands and fingers. Some viewers pointed to what they perceived as missing fingers and strange hand transitions in the advert.

In an interview with Variety, Chomet and producer Aton Soumache insisted that the advert was hand-drawn and generative AI was never used. But they have confirmed using a process known as “automated interpolation” to generate intermediate frames as “a very small part of the process” for the “repetitive, mechanical part of animation, not the creative work”. Automated interpolation is a standard digital animation tool that precedes AI, but now often involves its use.

The Dior case is illustrative of how vigilant audiences have become about AI use. Just as the presence of deepfakes risks undermining our trust in all images online, a few undisclosed AI-produced adverts can lead to scepticism of all advertising as viewers hunt for evidence of brands cutting corners rather than hiring creatives.
Even when specific accusations prove unfounded, the broader shift in advertising toward undisclosed generative AI raises deeper ethical and aesthetic questions for the industry as a whole.
AI models are often trained on artists’ work without compensation and threaten to put them out of work – not to mention AI datacentres’ impact on communities and the environment.

There’s also an irony in major brands baulking at the tedious task of getting the details right, and giving a misleading impression of fully human creation. These moral defects can diminish our aesthetic experience of AI adverts.

But putting aside morality, the revelation of AI use renders ads aesthetically worse in another way. Philosophers of art argue that forgeries are worse as artworks because they misrepresent achievement. We usually appreciate what the artist did in creating a work. So when we learn that a painting is not a genuine Vermeer, but a 20th century forgery by Van Meegeren, we judge it differently. (One philosopher even likens this betrayal to sexual infidelity – perhaps a bit much!)

Similarly, when we discover a beautiful, animated Christmas ad was produced with AI, we might lose appreciation for its creative process. The appearance of delicately hand-animated characters is a façade, generated not by artistic imagination but raw computational power. It’s not fraud, but it diminishes the experience.

Using AI to assist in creating complex scenery isn’t easy, and there can be skill to its use – some philosophers liken it to gardening. But it’s not the real process of hand-drawing and animation. To present it as such is a misrepresentation of achievement, imitating a style without the requisite labour behind it.

In response to these quandaries, some brands have taken to detailing the human processes behind their animated Christmas ads. Prada’s campaign emphasises traditional hand-drawn animation, with a separate behind-the-scenes video highlighting its artists. Others have followed suit. Barbour and Thatchers Cider each employed Aardman (producers of Wallace & Gromit) to hand-animate their adverts, while Etsy’s festive campaign is not-so-subtly titled “celebrate being human”. There are also video game studios which have detailed their refusal to use generative AI.

The praise showered on these traditional productions proves that audiences still care deeply about craft. A season built on warmth and sincerity cannot be manufactured by an algorithm that has never felt either.
Alex Fisher has received research funding from the Society for Applied Philosophy, the Leverhulme Trust, the Aristotelian Society, and the Royal Institute of Philosophy.

articles.title: The nine best books with yearning protagonists for readers who are pining
articles.author: Sarah Olive, Senior Lecturer in Literature, Aston University
paras: There is nothing like the agonising yet delicious slow burn of wanting someone you cannot have. Yearning is behind many great romance tropes, from the tragedy of “right person, wrong time” to the tension of “will they, won’t they”.
The cultural critic bell hooks saw yearning as a universal human condition, which could range from a “passionate collective longing for peace and justice” to an individual longing for a lover.

Yearning is a tradition that has flourished in English literature since 18th-century romanticism, a movement that celebrated the personal and the emotional. For such bittersweet desire to take root, there must be a significant hurdle that makes togetherness seem unattainable. That obstacle can take many forms: unrequited affection, painful shyness, or forces external to the pair.

In literature, these commonly include social stigma, geographical distance and mortality. Whatever the barrier, both it and the longing between the two characters must endure. Suspended between memory and fantasy, caught between a lost past and an imagined future, yearning should consume vast amounts of time and energy. The author must allow the reader to access the inner workings of the pining protagonist, so we can sit with their ache and share it.
If you are ready to luxuriate in the angst, here are nine books to pine over.

No one’s 20s and 30s look the same. You might be saving for a mortgage or just struggling to pay rent. You could be swiping dating apps, or trying to understand childcare. No matter your current challenges, our Quarter Life series has articles to share in the group chat, or just to remind you that you’re not alone.
Five ways to find your personal style outside of trends and algorithms
The ick: the psychology of why a romantic partner can suddenly repulse you
Should you cut off your friend? How to tell when a friendship needs repair, change or an ending
1. Eugene Onegin by Alexander Pushkin (1833)

Two of the book’s characters experience yearning and rejection: cosmopolitan Onegin and country girl Tatyana. Moreover, both characters get a turn at being the pursuer and the pursued in their taut encounters.
Pushkin wrote in Russian. English-language translations variously convey the book’s historic and contemporary qualities.

But if they smack too much of the 19th-century for you, try Clémentine Beauvais’ young adult reimagining, In Paris with You (2018). It transposes the story to 21st-century France. Like the original, it tells the story through the medium of poetry, rather than prose.
2. Love in the Time of Cholera by Gabriel García Márquez (1985)
García Márquez won the Nobel prize for literature in 1982. But the yearning in this Colombian novel deserves an endurance award of its own.
Rejected by the beautiful, young Fermina Daza, trainee telegraph operator Florentino Ariza nevertheless continues to love her for 51 years, nine months and four days.

This does not, however, prevent him from having an enjoyable sex life over the decades. In depicting this, the book underscores that yearning and sexual desire are not synonymous. It is just one way in which the book offers an ultimately hopeful take on an initially tortuous experience.
3. Bel Canto by Ann Patchett (2001)

Also set in South America, the action of Bel Canto is condensed into a few months rather than half a century. Events feel further compressed as they occur under a single roof, in an embassy full of guests taken hostage by revolutionaries.

The hostages are initially kept in cramped conditions, under the watchful eyes of the guards. Language barriers abound as captives from an array of nations work through a single translator. For these reasons, the relationships smoulder before consummation.

Some of the yearnings arise within the group of hostages, others between hostages and their captors. However, they are not limited to the sexual or romantic. They include longings for freedom, home and the characters’ previously mundane lives.
4. The Gift of Rain by Tan Twan Eng (2007)
Malaysian novelist Tan Twan Eng should earn a triple entry in this list because yearning is a staple of his writing.
The longings in three of his books (The Gift of Rain, The Garden of Evening Mists and The House of Doors) eschew yearning that is narrowly romantic or erotic for something more ambiguous.

The stories are steeped in the complex social and political contexts of their setting in colonial and wartime Malaya. The yearnings are straight and queer, familial and national, and treacherous for the characters in both political and personal ways.
5. The Painted Veil by Somerset Maugham (1925)

Eng’s novel The House of Doors takes inspiration from Somerset Maugham’s life and works. These include The Letter (1926) and The Painted Veil (1925). That book gets its own entry here for its plot of yearning that jumps tracks from the selfish to the selfless, the unworthy to the worthwhile.
That may sound moralistic, but the novel mines many grey areas as young socialite Kitty Fane searches for meaning in her life as a doctor’s wife in cholera-ridden rural China.
There’s also a gorgeous film adaptation from 2006 to enjoy once you’ve read the book.
6. Under the Udala Trees by Chinelo Okparanta (2015)

Yearning is a characteristic strongly associated with queer literature. This is unsurprising given the legal, religious and cultural prohibitions of, and discrimination against, same-sex relationships.

The publication of homoerotic literature in such contexts required that authors finely balance expression and suppression. Building on hooks’ work, literature professor Elleke Boehmer argues that a “rarefied intensity of desire” emerges in repressive contexts.

Under the Udala Trees is set in one such context, the 1960s Nigerian civil war. The protagonist, Ijeoma, pines first for a classmate, then for a customer. Yet arguably her greatest longing is for self-acceptance and her mother’s acceptance of her sexuality.
7. The End of the Affair by Graham Greene (1951)
The heart-wrenching yearning in this novel comes in the aftermath of an ecstatic affair, with writer Maurice still pining for married Sarah Miles.
Maurice assumes Sarah has forsaken him for her dutiful but dull husband, Henry. But the eventual plot twist that follows is sharper than a hairpin bend.

The novel is one of several by Greene with a strong Catholic focus. As such, the lovers’ relationships with God form a second triangle in this book. Ultimately, Maurice discovers his true rival is not Henry, but the Almighty himself, transforming an obsessive tale of earthly adultery into an agonising collision between human desire and divine grace.
8. Wuthering Heights by Emily Brontë (1847)
“Haunt me then … drive me mad! Only do not leave me in this abyss, where I cannot find you!”

Wuthering Heights is a tale of dark, destructive yearning across several generations of the same two families. It is also widely found on school curricula, so film versions abound. These include Emerald Fennell’s 2026 movie released to coincide with Valentine’s day, proving that the novel’s afterlife is as perverse as its plot and characters.

If you’re looking for a barrier to true love rooted more explicitly in the supernatural, Stephanie Meyer’s third novel in the Twilight saga, Eclipse (2007), draws strongly on Brontë’s love-triangle classic.
9. Mr Loverman by Bernadine Evaristo (2013)

This novel is a reminder that you are never too old to yearn. Or perhaps, that age is a spur to acting on your feelings. Mr Loverman vies with Love in a Time of Cholera for endurance but exhibits a lighter, more worldly-wise tone throughout.

It spans greater distances, from Antigua to Hackney. Barrington’s wife suspects he is consumed with extramarital passion. She manages to indict most of their acquaintances, except the real object of his affection. The book is unashamedly humorous and poignant. The BBC adapted it as a mini-series in 2024.

articles.title: How poetry can offer a vital, humane response to dementia
articles.author: Kevin Harvey, Associate Professor in Sociolinguistics, University of Nottingham
paras: I’m sitting in the lounge of a Midlands nursing home on a hazy September morning. Most of the residents here have dementia and, as in many care and nursing homes, they lack meaningful ways to spend their time.

People are dozing in armchairs or, if awake, enduring the vacuous assault of daytime television. One resident is confused and unable to settle. “I want to go home,” she cries over and over, “I want to go home!”
The scene hardly seems conducive to a quiet poetry reading.

But when I start to read a poem aloud (John Masefield’s Sea-Fever, 1902), something happens. First, there’s a near-collective stirring: heads lift and turn towards me. Then, after picking up the thread, several residents start to recite the poem for themselves, summoning words first encountered over 60 years ago but still recalled with facility and aplomb.
Soon there are stories of long-lost seaside memories. Fish and chips on Cromer Pier. Fusty old guest houses. Slippery shingles beneath the feet.
For the first time this morning, there’s laughter in the room.

It doesn’t always happen like this. But whenever I read poetry aloud in dementia care homes, I’m struck by the influence it has on people’s quality of life – how dementia gives way to the person, revealing the self beneath.

Research suggests that shared reading can improve the wellbeing of people with dementia, encouraging engagement, enjoyment and reminiscence. One study found lower dementia symptom scores during a programme of group reading, alongside reports of improved listening, memory and attention.

The human response to poetry, it seems, continues to exist at a fundamental level. When interviewing the former poet laureate Andrew Motion for my book The Literary Lifeline about the power of reading in helping people cope in hard times, he said: “Our brains are hardwired to retain and enjoy the characteristic features of poetry … We are a poetic species. Poetry is like breathing to us.”
But what is it, exactly, about poetry that lends itself to enduring recall and cognitive stimulation?

The poet Don Paterson described a poem as “a little machine for remembering itself” (itself a memorable formulation). “The memory of a symphony, painting, film or novel,” he writes, “is no more than that: just a memory, or at best a very partial recovery. But if you remember a poem, you possess it wholly. To recall a poem is the poem; the poem has become, quite literally, part of your being.”
It’s perhaps no wonder, then, that poems known by heart remain with us, even in the face of progressive cognitive decline. The neural basis for such retention, however, is not fully understood.

Poetry may be particularly memorable because its rhythm, metre and patterns of sound give words a structure that resembles music. In one experiment, researchers found that people retained the precise wording of poems better than prose over short periods of time. Whether this advantage also helps people with dementia recall familiar poems remains an open question.

Some musical abilities can remain relatively intact in people with dementia, even in its later stages. For example, research has found that some people with severe Alzheimer’s disease can still recall familiar melodies when prompted by their lyrics, and recognise familiar song lyrics.

Poetry’s patterns of sound may also help make words more memorable. In experiments, researchers found that alliteration – the repetition of similar sounds – could prompt people to recall previously encountered information.

Arts interventions such as music and poetry therapy not only stimulate the mind; they can also help reduce anxiety and agitation in dementia, offering, in milder cases of disruption, a more humane alternative to antipsychotic medication. These drugs treat the symptoms of distress, whereas non-pharmacological interventions respond to the whole person and their environment – to unmet needs that might be driving the agitation in the first place.
So extending arts activities in dementia care could help reduce the use of antipsychotic medication, which are often over-used in care homes and can decrease quality of life.

Of course, not everyone enjoys or positively responds to poetry and the arts. “It’s like being back at bloody school!” one unimpressed care-home resident harrumphed while I was reciting Alfred Tennyson’s Crossing the Bar (1889) and William Wordsworth’s Daffodils (also known as I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud, 1804).

Nevertheless, the value and power of poetry in dementia care homes is often under-appreciated and overlooked. A few years ago, I gave a quavering talk on poetry at a regional dementia forum. During the conference reception, I was approached by an immaculately dressed, red-faced man.
“You shouldn’t have given that talk,” he said.
Here we go, I thought. Brace yourself. (Throughout the day I’d been accosted by delegates with their public speaking advice.)
“I looked after my wife for 13 years,” he said, his voice faltering. “I played music to her, sang with her, went dancing with her. But I never read poetry to her.”
“She would’ve loved that.”

articles.title: While the term ‘Friendsgiving’ is new, the tradition has been around for decades – found family and experimental freedom make this holiday special
articles.author: Kirsten Chervenak, Research Associate for the Center for Regional Agriculture, Food, and Transformation, Chatham University
paras: One of my favorite holiday memories is of a Friendsgiving my husband and I hosted in our tiny two-bedroom house in Atlanta. We didn’t have a dining room. We barely had space to fit a foldout table in the living room. I think one of us sat in an office chair because we didn’t have enough seating. But having our friends gather in our home, no matter how small, made me feel proud.

I planned the menu for weeks, grocery shopped far in advance, and spent days prepping. As a young adult hosting my first holiday, I felt a lot of pressure to get it right. But I also reveled in the freedom to make it what I envisioned. I deviated from traditional family dishes, made impressive magazine cover desserts, and bought linens and dishware to create a tablescape.
While I knew I couldn’t recreate the grandness of my grandma’s family gatherings, I wanted this one to reflect my taste.

My inclination to host a gathering that honors the holiday while making the presentation my own may feel familiar. While many people grow up with certain familial obligations around holidays, entrance into adulthood may grant you some liberties from them, or at least some agency on whether to participate in the production of the event.
If you’re looking to assert that agency, Friendsgiving is the perfect holiday.

As a food studies scholar researching how food traditions are shared and preserved, I am interested in the idea of a holiday that centers friends over kin. I think this is why Friendsgiving, a term that emerged only in the early 2000s even though people had been participating in the concept long before, endures as a sanctified gathering.
Not your grandma’s dinner party

Modern American dinner parties still have roots in the Victorian era, when a formal gathering was steeped in etiquette and tradition to demonstrate class and propriety and to create social connections to improve one’s status. And while some form of social connection is still likely the main reason for gatherings today, dinner parties can take on many forms, often with the intention of sharing the labor involved.

In her book “Eating Together: Food, Friendship, and Inequality,” sociologist Alice P. Julier interviewed people of various classes, ages, incomes, sexualities, ethnicities and genders about mainly non-kin gatherings around food. Different forms of gathering require different amounts of labor – sometimes paid labor – and the labor between couples and friends is often negotiated. But she found that women often still took on the bulk of the work in the planning, communication or execution of an event.

Within these circumstances, the women often navigated this labor in ways that worked for them or fit their ideas around work, femininity and hospitality. As a young woman, I wanted to emulate the holidays I had experienced, hosted by my mother and grandmother, and was happy to take on the labor involved. However, the beauty of a Friendsgiving is that this labor can be shared and divided in accordance with capacity.

Friends who don’t enjoy cooking can provide drinks or snacks, while those – like me – who spend their days scouring food magazines can try out a new recipe. The key is being honest about the time and money you are able to spend and fit the gathering to the needs of the group.

No one’s 20s and 30s look the same. You might be saving for a mortgage or just struggling to pay rent. You could be swiping dating apps or trying to understand childcare. No matter your current challenges, our Quarter Life series has articles to share in the group chat, or just to remind you that you’re not alone.
What’s your apocalypse skill? Finding a future‑proof hobby can bring fulfilment today
Five ways to enjoy fashion as a hobby without indulging in overconsumption
The ick: The psychology of why a romantic partner can suddenly repulse you
A holiday that expands boundaries
Today, Thanksgiving is typically viewed as a family holiday.
For some, this may be the gathering that provides the warm, fuzzy holiday feeling many search for. But for others, family holidays are stressful.
A 2023 survey of 2,061 adults found that 9 in 10 people reported experiencing stress around money, lost loved ones, familial conflict or other expectations during the holidays.
As Friendsgiving isn’t an established holiday, participation is difficult to capture. But of 1,000 people surveyed in 2024, 20% said they planned to celebrate Friendsgiving.
A Friendsgiving is the opposite of established kin-keeping traditions. It gives the opportunity to gather with found family, and while the reason for gathering is established, the form is malleable.

Many people choose a potluck-style as a way of sharing the burden for what can be a labor-intensive meal. Others choose to do away entirely with what is considered the “traditional” meal and showcase foods from their own culture or a cuisine they enjoy.

As a parody of a holiday, Friendsgiving gives participants permission to make the holiday their own and be as playful as they wish. So, if I burn my miso butter corn casserole, no one will be disappointed, because they’ve never tasted it before anyway.
How to host a successful Friendsgiving
While playing with form and bucking traditional structure can be rewarding, there are some things you may want to keep in mind to have a successful Friendsgiving.

In her book “The Art of Gathering: How We Meet and Why it Matters,” author Priya Parker advises anyone planning a gathering to be specific about purpose. This will help decide the form of the event and whom to invite.

Is this a casual gathering with friends? Is fellowship or food more important? Are you hoping to try a recipe your family would never approve? Be specific about your own expectations before you start planning.

The Emily Post Institute, which promotes etiquette and offers resources for a variety of social situations, recommends being flexible with the menu. This is especially important for a potluck-style gathering. As a host, you may want to assign dishes to guests to ensure a balanced meal without eight desserts. If you have the gumption, however, you can throw caution to the wind and see what happens.
It is also important to keep dietary restrictions in mind to make sure everyone feels included and has something to eat.
Make a plan for heating or reheating. The oven is prime real estate during Thanksgiving. You may want to tell guests to bring their dish already cooked to avoid playing oven Tetris.
Finally, tell guests to bring Tupperware. There will be leftovers, and I have found that nothing is better than creating a second plate to take home and heat up the next day.
Alice P. Julier, a professor of food studies at Chatham University, assisted with the writing of this article.
Kirsten Chervenak is a past student of Alice Julier

articles.title: Jensen Huang scandal illustrates why human nature is cybersecurity’s weakest link
articles.author: Vanessa Bohns, Braunstein Family Professor and Chair of Organizational Behavior, Cornell University
paras: The end of Jensen Huang’s tenure at Nvidia is steeped in irony. The chief executive of a company whose growth has been propelled by the seemingly unstoppable rise of artificial intelligence was brought down by a vulnerability that no algorithm can eliminate: human nature.

Huang’s resignation from the chipmaker he co-founded followed reports of multiple affairs, most notably one with Alice Huang, a business executive whom U.S. authorities suspect of spying for China. The company says no secrets were leaked.

In a world increasingly focused on protecting private information against high-tech hacking schemes, Huang’s downfall is a reminder that, as the infamous hacker Kevin Mitnick observed, the “human factor is truly security’s weakest link.”

Huang is hardly the first person in a powerful position to lower their defenses. In 2023, Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni spoke candidly about foreign affairs in a call with Russian pranksters who recorded and released the conversation. In 2011, former CIA Director David Petraeus gave his biographer, with whom he was having an affair, access to notebooks containing classified information.
These cases raise an important question: Why would someone with an entire security apparatus at their disposal let their guard down in an ordinary conversation or an intimate moment?

Part of the answer comes down to the ways in which we are wired to react to other human beings. As a social psychologist who studies how people respond to requests, I’ve seen how a human voice, a simple touch or the mere physical presence of another person can be persuasive. Social cues that increase a sense of familiarity and intimacy can make people feel safer, more trusting – and more willing to hand over money, comply with requests, divulge information or take risks.
The comfort of a human voice

Mitnick has been called “the most notorious hacker of all time.” Until his arrest in 1995, he spent years gaining access to privileged information at companies such as Nokia and Motorola. He pulled off his espionage not by writing sophisticated code-breaking software but by having conversations with his targets.
He would call people up and talk them into handing over their passwords by claiming to be the new IT guy or someone’s boss’s colleague. The people he spoke to overwhelmingly believed him.
In other words, Mitnick recognized the power of the human voice.

Studies show that hearing a person’s voice, as compared to reading their written thoughts, makes that person seem more capable and relatable. Interactions via phone, video chat and voice chat also create stronger social bonds than the same kinds of interactions via text or email.

Perhaps for these reasons, people are more effective at persuading others to do things for them over the phone compared to when they make the same requests by text. In a study I conducted with social psychologist Mahdi Roghanizad, participants asked other people for favors through randomly assigned communication channels. They received about twice as many “yes” responses over the phone as they did by email.
When it comes to obtaining company secrets or circumventing export laws, a human voice may be all you need. And that isn’t the only edge people have.
Studies have found that human touch can also have surprising effects on tipping behavior, acquiescence and risk-taking.

In a famous 1984 study, a server who lightly touched diners as she handed them their change received bigger tips. In another classic psychology study, female experimenters approached 178 strangers and asked them for change to use a nearby pay phone. When the experimenters lightly touched the arm of a person they approached, that person was 76% more likely to agree to give the change.
The researchers theorized that these light touches created a sense of familiarity. That familiarity, in turn, made people more willing to open their wallets.

Other research suggests that light touch can also make people feel safer and more willing to take risks. In a 2010 study, participants were more willing to take financial risks when a female experimenter gave them a light, comforting pat on their shoulder.

Perhaps the most well-known study of influence, Stanley Milgram’s infamous shock experiment, illustrates how much it can matter to be in the room when you ask someone to do something they may be feeling uneasy about.

In the original study, an experimenter stood behind participants and instructed them to administer purportedly dangerous shocks to someone they thought was just another participant. The experimenter asked participants to incrementally increase the intensity of the shocks. Nearly two-thirds of participants went all the way to the highest shock setting. In a variation of the study, however, the experimenter left the room and gave instructions over the phone. In this version, only 22.5% went that far.

Although researchers continue to debate how to interpret Milgram’s findings, my colleagues and I have similarly found that people are far more likely to say yes when we ask them to do something face-to-face.

In one study, participants who made requests in person were 34 times more likely to get a yes than those who made requests by email. In another study, in-person requests were significantly more effective than requests made over the phone or video call.

Cyberattacks and phishing emails pose real threats to security. But sometimes the biggest threats come from the people in the room with you. While we don’t know exactly what transpired between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, her proximity to the Nvidia CEO illustrates a vulnerability that even the best cybersecurity measures can struggle to guard against.

articles.title: The 12th-century Chinese poet who was among the first to explore the inner lives of cats
articles.author: Jack W. Chen, Professor of Chinese Literature, University of Virginia
paras: If you’re reading this, then your media feed, like mine, is probably full of cats.
That’s hardly surprising. The internet has always belonged to cats, which suits me just fine: I love cats and live with four of them.

But in one of the classes I’ve taught, Cats: Why We Love Them, I explain how our affection for the house cat, Felis silvestris catus, is a relatively recent phenomenon in the scope of human history. In many parts of the world, cats were viewed with suspicion and subjected to terrible mistreatment.

Of course, the ancient Egyptians loved cats – this can be seen in sculptures, paintings and even mummified cat remains. Meanwhile, premodern poets, writers and artists were among the first to wonder about the inner lives of cats – and to explore how caring for them might expand our capacity for empathy.

One of the earliest literary accounts of a cat is the ninth-century poem “Pangur Bán,” written by an unnamed Irish monk. In the poem, he describes the parallels between his devotion to hunting for meaning in the texts he is studying and the cat’s devotion to hunting mice.

What’s interesting about the poem is how the anonymous poet sees the cat as possessing qualities that resemble human qualities – and, in doing so, implicitly suggests that cats have dignity much like human dignity.
The monk does not set himself above the cat in some great hierarchy of life, but instead places himself alongside the cat as peers in their dedicated practices.

In the 12th century, the Chinese poet Lu You composed over 9,000 poems. A handful were about his cats, and of these, three are entitled “Zeng mao,” or “Presented to My Cat.” It’s not clear if the poems are all about the same cat, as Lu had more than one cat over his lifetime.

In Chinese literature, poems that include the term “zeng” – “to present” – are often sent to acquaintances as a form of literary exchange. Prior to Lu, there’s no literary evidence that anyone had addressed a poem to a cat.
In the first poem, Lu begins by explaining that he acquired a cat to protect his library from vermin. Looking around his home, he feels embarrassed by his lack of success in life:
I’m ashamed that I’m poor and my achievements few, When you’re cold there’s no rug, when I feed you there’s no fish.
In the second of these poems, a longer eight-line poem, the poet accuses his cat of poor feline behavior familiar even today:
You frequently get drunk from catnip, You commandeer the blanket every night.
But he follows with praise for the cat’s achievements:
Deeds of the mousehole – just now recounted, Rewards of fish morsels – how could these be omitted?
He ends by naming the cat:
Still, I should give you a name, I’ll call you “Little Tiger.”

Lu chooses a name that probably was given to countless cats in premodern China. But by ending the poem with the act of naming, he is emphasizing how this cat is an individual to him, known to him by this name and none other.
Poet and cat, late in life
The relationship that Lu depicts between cat and human will be familiar to anyone who has fought with their cat over who gets the blanket or wondered what their cat might be thinking.

The third poem, translated here in full, finds the cat late in its life, with its days chasing mice long behind it. Its poignancy is amplified by the fact that Lu composed it in the last year of his own life:
As for catching mice you lack merit, but I never complain, A ladle of fish and rice will come at the usual time. Throughout the day I see you sleeping peacefully, So why am I always coming and going?

Lu sees himself through the bemused eyes of the cat, who’s perhaps wondering why this foolish old man is rushing to and fro, fulfilling goals and seeking praise, when he might just be satisfied with what he already has.

And despite his cat’s indolence, Lu continues to cherish his feline, making sure to regularly serve its dinner. This is significant, given that other premodern Chinese writers viewed cats primarily as vermin-catchers that should be replaced once they outlive their usefulness.

Imagining oneself as a pampered cat will be familiar to those of us who live with cats – a thought-experiment that is tinged with more than a little envy for the capacity to live in the moment, without anxiety over the future.

Lu’s care for his cat affords him the possibility of imagining a nonhuman animal mind. The poet learns something from his cat in the end, as he imagines the world through the cat’s eyes and, in doing so, perhaps finds a measure of solace.
Lu does not speak in the language of what philosophers call moral personhood. He is not reflecting on the broader ethical question of which creatures deserve to be treated with care and respect.

But I argue that his actions nonetheless demonstrate how he treats his cat as somewhat of an equal. This can be seen, not least of all, by how he addresses poems to his cat, an act of social exchange that was heretofore reserved for literary interactions with other human beings.

Personhood – the recognition of an individual as deserving of dignity – is often assumed the sole province of human beings. But philosopher María Puig de la Bellacasa has promoted a worldview that she calls “more than human thinking,” which urges people to broaden their scope of moral concern, and in this way, enlarge human capacities for care and love. The philosopher Lori Gruen similarly conceives of an “entangled empathy,” calling attention to the complex relational intimacies that bind human and nonhuman animals together. They insist that human lives are better when the sphere of care and concern is extended to those creatures with whom human lives are entangled.

Born in the 12th century, Lu You could not be expected to argue for animal rights. But he clearly understands that his cat has claims to happiness, pleasure, comfort and companionship, and that while the cat might see the world differently than he does, that doesn’t diminish its claim to empathy and love.

articles.title: Bond has always reflected the masculinity of his time – Robert Pattinson’s 007 will need to embody a new era
articles.author: Monica Germanà, Reader in Gothic and Contemporary Studies, University of Westminster
paras: James Bond has always reflected the cultural anxieties and zeitgeist of his era.

Sean Connery’s Bond embodied the confident western post-second-world-war masculinity of the early cold war. George Lazenby brought the character’s emotional vulnerability to light, reflecting the upheavals of the late 1960s. Roger Moore’s performance, meanwhile, added camp humour, theatricality and escapism in the 1970s.

In keeping with Ian Fleming’s more psychologically complex literary creation, Timothy Dalton brought a darker, more ruthless Bond to the screen. Stripping away much of the Moore era’s comedy and camp, his portrayal foregrounded emotional intensity and moral ambiguity. This reflected late-cold-war anxieties as geopolitical certainties unravelled and new threats emerged.

Next up, Pierce Brosnan incarnated a glamorous post-cold-war masculinity, with his lingering sexism teased out by Samantha Bond’s witty Moneypenny and the disruptive casting of Judi Dench as M, the head of MI6. And in the 2000s, Daniel Craig’s Bond was a physically tough but emotionally vulnerable character. His wounded body and scarred mind linked emotional detachment to childhood trauma.

Pattinson’s acting credentials make him one of the most established actors to take on the role. Since the Twilight saga (2008-2012), he has grown to be among the more versatile actors of his generation, with a penchant for challenging, often downright strange roles.

From the psychological intensity of Good Time (2017) to Robert Eggers’s claustrophobic gothic The Lighthouse (2018), the characters he has played are anything but straightforward leading men. Even when turning to action, his Batman (2022) was unexpectedly brooding and introspective.
There is certainly scope with his casting to extend the darker vision of Bond first introduced by Dalton and subsequently developed by Craig.

Visually, too, Pattinson seems almost a composite of previous Bonds. Declared the world’s most handsome man in 2020, Pattinson has the chiselled good looks of Brosnan. Although he might not have Connery’s physique, the intense training he underwent for Batman suggests that he could manage the demanding physical aspects of the role. This, however, may be more challenging, given that Pattinson, at 40, is already ten years older than former producer Barbara Broccoli had anticipated the next Bond would be in 2024.

As a white Englishman whose image is associated with an upper-middle-class, heterosexual masculinity, Pattinson might seem a safe, even predictable, choice for Bond. And yet, he is not unfamiliar with the challenge of portraying unconventional masculinity.

In Little Ashes (2008), he explored the young Salvador Dalí’s intimate relationship with the poet Federico García Lorca. Much like Craig, he has shown himself willing to explore queer desire and the instability of masculine identity.
I think what Craig’s era could have done more with is humour, and Pattinson might well bring a fresh comic sensibility to the next incarnation of Bond.

Beneath his often brooding intensity lies a nuanced comic performer. Humour has allowed Pattinson to question conventional masculinity in some of his roles. In Damsel (2018), he challenged the traditional western hero by playing an inept cowboy whose masculine confidence far exceeded his capabilities. Elsewhere, his darkly camp rendition of Louis the Dauphin in The King (2019), the tragi-comic The Drama (2026) and the self-aware short Fear & Shame (2017) all seemingly serve to undermine male vanity.

Perhaps Pattinson’s history of darkly strange and funny characters will create space for this new Bond to, playfully or otherwise, explore our current preoccupations with toxic masculinity, sexual consent and male vulnerability.

Fleming thought of his secret agent as an “unobtrusive … neutral figure – an anonymous blunt instrument”. Screenwriter Steven Knight now faces the challenge of using Bond as a blank canvas to highlight the clash between the character’s traditional roots and modern culture.
In particular, the new Bond would benefit from a more diverse supporting cast whose backgrounds are woven naturally into the story, reflecting his global audience without feeling forced.

I’m thinking female characters not defined by their relationships with Bond, villains who call out Bond’s elitism, queer characters that could complicate his seemingly straight world. Bond girls and villains will play a crucial role in delivering these (or failing to do so). But it will be Pattinson and his choices for this iconic character at the centre of it all, deciding whether the franchise will sink or swim.

articles.title: Robert Pattinson is the first Bond with a strong franchise history – it makes him a safe choice
articles.author: Yannis Tzioumakis, Professor of Film and Media Industries, University of Liverpool
paras: Robert Pattinson’s casting as the new Bond has been met with a mixed reaction across the internet.

For some, he has the looks and he can do action. He’s proven he can handle all kinds of villains who dream of world domination from the plotting, power-hungry Antinous in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey (2026) to corrupt, manipulative preacher Preston Teagardin in The Devil All the Time (2020).

I am not as convinced. But I was also happy to see someone cast that I’ve had good knowledge of as an actor. Perhaps more importantly, I was relieved to see that the choice involved a man who was in his 40s (only just). Being both a big fan of the series and much closer to Daniel Craig’s age myself, I was afraid that the new producers of the franchise would go down the (much) younger actor route.

The Bond series has historically been attracting more discerning and mature audiences than the Marvel and DC films or even the Star Wars franchise. I can imagine it might have been tempting for Amazon to try to entice the much coveted youth demographic through the choice of a young(er) Bond.

Still, the decision to cast Pattinson doesn’t seem to have been either easy or obvious. This is the first Bond played by an actor who was once a teen idol. It’s also the first Bond who has been a member of multiple other cinematic universes: from the Wizarding World (with a small but memorable part in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire) and the Twilight Saga (which he largely defined through his role as Edward Cullen) to the Batman Epic Crime Saga (as the titular superhero) and the Dune universe (portraying Scytale in the third instalment of that franchise). Now to the Bond universe.

Pattinson’s ability to seamlessly integrate himself into so many major story-worlds, in small parts and leading roles, as a hero and a villain, speaks volumes both to his skills as an actor and the characteristics of his star persona. He has proven himself an actor who is not as easy to pin down, especially when taking into consideration his more indie roles.

He’s had memorable performances in A24 titles such as The Lighthouse (2019), The Drama (2026) and Primetime (2026) and collaborations with art-house auteurs such as Bong Joon Ho (Mickey 17, 2025), David Cronenberg (Cosmopolis, 2012) and Fernando Meirelles (the upcoming The Take, 2027). These stints paint a picture of a highly unpredictable actor who can be at home in any kind of a project. The choices Pattinson makes with his projects speaks to his artistic sensibilities.

So he’s a global star and an indie darling. He’s the seasoned franchise professional and the artist with the ability to regenerate with every role. He’s also the 40-year old (although he claims he’s gen Z) who appeals to adults while continuing to have an extremely strong fan-base among young audiences – a performer approved by both children and parents.

It is perhaps such intriguing combinations that convinced Amazon MGM to cast him in the role of Bond. In doing so, Amazon went against long-standing casting practices in the franchise’s history of casting actors who were not incredibly well known yet or associated with other such well known characters or franchises.

Having had so far mixed results in extending franchises (The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power and Reacher) and with its production strategies increasingly focused on exploiting established intellectual property (with a reboot of Robocop also in development), Amazon could not afford to get Bond wrong. Casting Pattinson is a calculated risk that also fits well with the big tech company’s well-publicised identity as an innovator.

Casting Pattinson as 007 may not have been an obvious move, but it was the product of thinking outside the box and against established practices in the series and, arguably, in franchise casting more broadly.

Should the 26th Bond film be a box office hit and the entry point to a new chapter in the franchise’s history, it could be down to this clever pairing of a star for all seasons and a company that recognised his qualities and cast him (kind of) against the grain.

articles.title: In It, Pennywise the clown is a powerful metaphor for OCD
articles.author: Aisleen Sturrock, PhD Student in Creative Writing, Aberystwyth University
paras: Monsters are often used to represent mental health struggles, in both literature and film. These creatures often act as physical stand-ins for internal battles, giving shape to feelings that are usually invisible and hard to explain. By turning psychological distress into something audiences can see and react to, writers and filmmakers make those experiences easier to understand.

In the It franchise, the central monster is Pennywise the clown. In my research I seek to challenge the trivialisation of OCD by portraying the fear and complexity of living with the condition – and to deepen understanding of OCD themes through prose. While Stephen King’s original 1986 novel includes a complex mythology, I have found that the 2017 and 2019 film adaptations simplify Pennywise into a figure that works surprisingly well as a metaphor for obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD).

OCD is a condition in which a person experiences intense intrusive thoughts, known as obsessions. In response, people with OCD perform repetitive behaviours or mental acts called compulsions, to reduce distress or prevent a feared outcome. OCD can manifest itself through a range of different themes, often focusing on what someone values or fears most. For example, a person might worry they are a bad person because they dwell on a moment when they were slightly rude, or fear that stepping on a crack could harm a family member.

Eddie Kaspbrak, one of the main protagonists of King’s novel, experiences these kinds of compulsions. He has an intense fear of germs and illness that leads to a strong need for cleanliness, which he believes will prevent him from getting severe diseases.
This article is part of Rethinking the Classics. The stories in this series offer insightful new ways to think about and interpret classic books and artworks. This is the canon – with a twist.

Eddie fits with one of the most recognisable sub-types of the condition: contamination. This is a form of OCD in which someone believes that something has become contaminated by germs, illness, or even moral impurity such as sin. In response, they may engage in compulsive behaviour like frequent hand-washing, excessive cleaning of surfaces, or avoiding places and people they perceive as contaminated.

Played by Bill Skarsgård in the films It (2017) and It Chapter Two (2019), Pennywise’s strength builds from his ability to get into people’s heads. He feeds off the fear that grows through obsessions and remuneration. Remuneration is a compulsion in which a person repeatedly engages with intrusive thoughts, analysing them in an attempt to understand or resolve them. However this often makes the OCD cycle worse.
In It, the more the victim dwells on the fear, the stronger Pennywise becomes. This is similar to the way that when someone with OCD gives into their compulsions, their symptoms worsen.

Pennywise changes shape to match each child’s deepest fear. As the children become more frightened, he grows larger and more threatening. This mirrors the OCD cycle, where fear and avoidance reinforce intrusive thoughts, making them feel increasingly real and impossible to ignore.

In It: Chapter Two, Mike (Isaiah Mustafa) – one of the original frightened children, now a grown man – suggests that Pennywise knows “what scares [children] the most” and uses it to “salt the meat”. In both the film and novel, Pennywise appeared to Eddie as a diseased leper, directly targeting his intense fear of illness and contamination.

In the novel, Eddie experiences intrusive thoughts in his mother’s voice, something he calls his “mind-mother”. Eddie remembers his mother telling him he is “not like other people” and has “a very weak system,” reinforcing the idea that he is always at risk. Even after her death, her fears about sickness continue to control his behaviour. These internal warnings eventually become absurd in their extremity – “Eddie, get out of the taxi! They give you cancer!” – highlighting the exaggerated, catastrophic thinking typical of contamination OCD.

If Eddie’s mother’s voice represents his intrusive thoughts, then his inhaler (or his “aspirator”) is his compulsion. Even though, as an adult, he knows his inhaler was only ever a placebo, he still uses it in moments of stress. The irrationality of his fear doesn’t make it feel any less real.

In the novel, Eddie’s inhaler is repeatedly linked to violent imagery. In one section of the book, it is described like a weapon. Eddie stuffs it into his mouth and, “like miming suicide”, pulls “the trigger”. This unsettling comparison highlights how compulsions, while meant to provide relief, are harmful.

Later in the novel, Eddie’s compulsion of using his inhaler, meant to provide mental relief, is personified as a cruel voice that threatens him: “this time I might just kill ya!” This suggests that compulsions can become as frightening as the intrusive thoughts they are meant to control. Even knowing this, Eddie instinctively reaches for the inhaler, trapped in the familiar cycle of fear and temporary relief.
Eddie fights Pennywise and OCD

During the novel’s climax, Eddie turns his inhaler into a weapon against Pennywise, aiming it at the creature’s eyes. As he does, he imagines his mother’s voice warning him: “Don’t go near that Thing, Eddie! Things like that give you cancer!” This moment is important because Eddie doesn’t obey the intrusive thought – he challenges it. By using the object of his compulsion as a tool of resistance, Eddie symbolically pushes back against both his mother’s control and his disorder.

The final confrontation in the film adaptation It: Chapter Two (2019) also reflects real therapeutic ideas. Unlike in the novel, Pennywise isn’t defeated through brute force, but through psychological resistance.

The “losers” (as the kids describe themselves) insult and mock him, calling him “just a clown”. As they do, Pennywise physically shrinks and loses power. This mirrors Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP), a therapy which encourages patients to let obsessions occur without completing the compulsion. Once Pennywise is no longer feared, he collapses, much like OCD loses its hold when compulsions are resisted.

It works as a striking metaphor for OCD. Each character is attacked through their deepest fears, and the more those fears are fixated on, the stronger Pennywise becomes. By turning intrusive thoughts into literal monsters, It captures the intensity of OCD’s internal struggles and offers a deeper, more empathetic understanding of the disorder and its emotional weight.
